person.name: Divya Bhatia
person.school: St. Andrew's School, Delaware · Class of 2027
person.thesis: I study how matter moves: carbon into seawater, roots into mud, ideas into communities. And I study who is changed when it does.
person.lede: A high-school researcher working where chemistry, biology and engineering meet the people they affect. Scroll down: like an ocean receiving alkalinity, the page shifts as each piece is added.

projects.title: Ocean Alkalinity Enhancement
projects.setting: Harvard Pre-College Program · The Chemistry of a Human Earth
projects.collaborators: with Una · course instructor Ruth Tweedy
projects.question: Can adding alkalinity to seawater safely pull carbon dioxide out of the air, and can anyone prove that it worked?
projects.method: With Una, synthesized the current literature: the carbonate chemistry (how added base shifts the CO₂ ⇌ HCO₃⁻ ⇌ CO₃²⁻ equilibrium and lowers seawater pCO₂), geological analogues such as silicate weathering and the recovery after the PETM, three delivery routes (mineral dispersal, electrochemical splitting, alkaline industrial waste), the first permitted field trials, monitoring technology, and cost and scale estimates.
projects.result: The chemistry is well understood, but measurement is the bottleneck. Total-alkalinity sensors are not yet reliably available, so trials depend on robots and models to follow a plume through open water. In the sources reviewed, about 730 tonnes of CO₂ removal had been verified worldwide, against a theoretical potential of billions of tonnes per year. Costs were roughly $250–850 per tonne, with projections of $50–160.
projects.impact: Coastal ecosystems and the people who depend on them carry the local risks of a pH shift. Honest monitoring is what makes the approach fair, not just effective.

projects.title: Why Cattails Stop at the Shoreline
projects.question: Cattails crowd the edges of the retention pond but never reach the middle. Why?
projects.method: Tested depth first: measured 80–106 cm at cattail sites and compared against peers' bathymetric map of the pond. Depth did not explain the pattern. Then designed a probe (after rejecting prototypes that were too flexible or too blunt) and recorded the force needed to push it into the pond bottom across four zones, coding readings below 40 N, 40–50 N, and 50 N or more.
projects.result: Cattails grew where the bottom was soft and mucky, and depth was ruled out. The project won Curiosity Quest Night in May 2024. The next open question: why are the near-shore zones soft in the first place?
projects.impact: Retention ponds exist to slow and clean stormwater for the neighborhoods around them. Knowing where wetland plants can take root helps the people who design and care for these ponds.

projects.title: Pick a Side: The Greenhouse Effect
projects.setting: Harvard Pre-College Program · The Chemistry of a Human Earth
projects.question: Can making classmates choose between a fact and a convincing misconception help them actually unlearn the misconception?
projects.method: Built paired claims, one accurate and one a common misconception, on the questions people most often get wrong: Earth's temperature without the greenhouse effect, whether gases trap sunlight or outgoing heat, the most abundant greenhouse gas, why industry switched from wood to coal, and why CO₂ outlasts methane. Each answer was backed by a cited source such as NASA or NCSE.
projects.result: A ready-to-run class activity. Try a few of the questions in the Curiosities section below.
projects.impact: Climate decisions are made by the public, not just by scientists. Clearing up one misconception at a time is part of the work.

projects.title: NorthStar*
projects.setting: Kode With Klossy · AI & Machine Learning capstone
projects.question: Can an AI guide recommend real places to eat and things to do in any city, without making places up?
projects.method: Built a Gradio chatbot on Hugging Face using retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). A large language model (Qwen 2.5, 7B) first turns a casual message into structured preferences: city, price, meal, food or activities, and whether the user wants more options. The app then pulls live places from the Foursquare Places API, caches results to avoid repeat calls, and falls back to a saved Yelp dataset when live data is unavailable. Only those retrieved places are handed back to the model to write the reply, five at a time.
projects.result: A deployed, streaming chatbot that remembers the city and request across a conversation and pages through new options on request. When it has no data, it says so instead of guessing.
projects.impact: Chatbots that invent restaurants can send someone across an unfamiliar city for nothing. Grounding every answer in real data, and admitting when there is none, is what makes a recommendation trustworthy.

projects.title: Hearing Hand
projects.setting: Kode With Klossy · Mobile App Development
projects.collaborators: built with a team of Kode With Klossy classmates
projects.question: Could learning American Sign Language feel as motivating as a language app, while teaching the culture behind the language and not just the signs?
projects.method: Designed and built a SwiftUI app in Xcode with the team. It has lessons on the alphabet and basic words, two quiz tracks (fingerspelling and everyday words), and a motivation system of streaks, gems and hearts. Deaf culture lessons on history, values and cultural behaviors sit alongside the vocabulary.
projects.result: A working iOS prototype in which culture lessons are part of the main path, not an appendix.
projects.impact: It treats Deaf culture as a culture, so learners meet its history, values and etiquette in the same place they learn the alphabet.

projects.title: Period 5
projects.collaborators: with Audrey, Marine and a third teammate
projects.question: Many young people who menstruate get little or no real education about their cycles. How do you give curious youth clear, friendly information they can actually use?
projects.method: Co-developed a website in HTML, CSS and JavaScript with fun facts about the menstrual cycle, trusted resources, and step-by-step instructions for using different period products.
projects.result: A working website, pitched to the rest of the Kode With Klossy scholars at the end of the program.
projects.impact: Menstrual health is often taught late, briefly, or not at all. Plain, judgment-free information helps young people understand their own bodies without embarrassment.

projects.title: The Planned Partition
projects.question: How did British policy in Punjab, from 1858 to 1947, turn a diverse population that had resisted together in 1857 into rigid political communities, and how did that contribute to the violence of 1947?
projects.method: Traced the argument through primary sources: the 573-page 1881 Census of Panjab, the Indian Councils Act of 1909, Mountbatten's June 1947 broadcast, 1947 newspaper reports of the train massacres, and the Stanford 1947 Partition oral-history archive. These were read alongside secondary historians.
projects.result: Argues that the census did not just record caste and religion, but fixed them into countable, comparable categories. Those categories later structured religious representation in government, making separation administrable long before it was violent.
projects.impact: Partition displaced millions and its divisions still shape South Asia. Understanding how categories become borders helps people resist the same process now.

projects.title: A Race Against Time: Partition of India, 1947
projects.collaborators: Chair; dais with a vice-chair and crisis director
projects.question: How do you let delegates feel the pressure of 1947 (collapsing authority, border uncertainty, rising violence) without already knowing how it ends?
projects.method: Wrote the background guide covering the crisis, the historical context, member descriptions and committee goals. Then chaired the crisis committee, in which delegates had no knowledge of how events actually unfolded.
projects.result: A full crisis committee of about 15 delegates, run as part of a progression from Vice Chair to Chair to Crisis Director.
projects.impact: Delegates practiced the empathy and judgment the guide asks for: historical curiosity, applied to a real human toll.

projects.title: Accent Magazine
projects.setting: Asian Student Union, St. Andrew's School
projects.collaborators: with fellow ASU co-heads; 19 student contributors in Issue 04, 11 in Issue 05
projects.question: What does it mean to be Asian in 21st-century America, told by the students living it?
projects.method: Created, edited and designed two editions of the ASU art and literary magazine, collecting student art, poetry and personal writing. Also contributed a poem, “Unboxed.”
projects.result: Two published editions (2024–25 and 2025–26). Alongside the magazine, ASU raised $500 for relief efforts after anti-Asian violence.
projects.impact: In the magazine's own words: “By sharing our voices, we become more resilient and powerful.”

archive.intro: Two timelines, kept side by side because they inform each other: the history Divya studies, and the community she helps build.

history.title: The Indian Rebellion
history.text: Hindu and Muslim soldiers rose against East India Company rule together, a unity the British would work to prevent from happening again.

history.title: Census of Panjab
history.text: The first synchronous census sorted every person by caste, religion and region, turning identities into fixed numbers.

history.title: Indian Councils Act
history.text: Expanded Indian participation in councils, but under rules that wrote religious division into representation.

history.title: Partition
history.text: Two nations were born on August 15. Months of violence followed, including the train massacres across the new border.

elements.name: Harvard Pre-College
elements.detail: Chemistry track: The Chemistry of a Human Earth (CHEM P-13010), a two-week course on pollution, climate and the chemistry of sustainable solutions.
details: A two-week college-level course (CHEM P-13010, July 20–31, 2026) that builds from first principles of chemistry to the largest environmental questions of the day: ocean acidification, carbon dioxide release, microplastics, and the chemistry of sustainable solutions. Each class applied chemistry to a different real-world case study.
Two projects came out of it: a final research synthesis on ocean alkalinity enhancement with Una, and *Pick a Side*, an interactive greenhouse-effect lesson with Camila.
elements.impact: Researching ocean carbon removal and the company Ebb Carbon turned a general interest in chemistry into a specific direction: climate, ocean science, and the chemistry of carbon removal.

elements.name: SCCUR 2026
elements.detail: Abstract on ocean alkalinity enhancement (with Una) submitted to the Southern California Conferences for Undergraduate Research.
details: Abstract submitted to the Southern California Conferences for Undergraduate Research (SCCUR) 2026, based on the ocean alkalinity enhancement (OAE) synthesis with Una.

The work explains how adding alkalinity shifts seawater’s carbonate equilibrium so the ocean absorbs more CO₂. It also covers the first permitted field trials (Ebb Carbon and Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution) and why monitoring, reporting and verification is the field’s main bottleneck.
elements.impact: Carbon removal only counts if it can be verified. The abstract centers that question for an undergraduate research audience. Status: submitted, decision pending.

elements.name: The Planned Partition
elements.detail: AS Research Seminar paper on caste, religion and colonial policy in Punjab, 1858–1947.
details: A 21-page AS Research Seminar paper (May 2026), including bibliography. It argues that after the 1857 rebellion, British policy in Punjab turned a diverse population into rigid political communities.

Its central primary source is the 573-page 1881 Census of Panjab, read alongside the Indian Councils Act of 1909, Mountbatten’s June 1947 broadcast, 1947 newspaper reports of the train massacres, and oral histories from Stanford’s 1947 Partition archive.
elements.impact: It shows how counting people can become dividing them, a question that reaches well beyond 1947.

elements.detail: Original poem by Divya, published in Accent, Issue 04 (2024–25).
details: An original poem published in *Accent*, Issue 04 (2024–25). It pushes back on the boxes people put her in, drawing on Bhangra, chai steeped with memory, and the meaning of her name.
It closes: “Call me what you want, I’ll still rise, / Feet to the drum, fire in my eyes.”
elements.impact: The same question that runs through her history research, how categories get assigned to people, told in the first person.

questions.q: Why are the near-shore zones of the pond soft in the first place?
How do you verify a chemical change in water that never stops moving?
Can carbon removal get cheap enough to matter without cutting corners on monitoring?
When a census counts people, when does counting become dividing?
What gets lost when a language is taught without its culture?

pickASide.prompt: Without the greenhouse effect, Earth's average surface temperature would…
pickASide.why: Greenhouse gases are why Earth averages about 15 °C instead of about −18 °C.

pickASide.prompt: Greenhouse gases warm the planet by…
options: trapping sunlight inside the atmosphere, like a glass greenhouse
absorbing the heat Earth radiates back toward space
pickASide.why: Sunlight mostly passes through. The gases absorb outgoing infrared heat, so the glass-greenhouse picture is misleading.

pickASide.prompt: The most abundant greenhouse gas in Earth's atmosphere is…
pickASide.why: Water vapor is the most abundant, and it amplifies warming started by CO₂.

pickASide.prompt: Methane traps ~80× more heat than CO₂ over 20 years. CO₂ is still the bigger long-term threat because…
options: methane breaks down in roughly 7–12 years, while CO₂ accumulates for generations
CO₂ absorbs high-energy sunlight that methane can't
pickASide.why: Methane reacts with OH radicals and breaks down within about a decade, while CO₂ keeps piling up.
